sources.headline: Audio reveals exchanges between Spain train operators and drivers moments before deadly crash
sources.text: Figure caption, Listen: Audio recordings between train driver and controllerByHarry Sekulich and Jaroslav LukivLeaked audio recordings that were published in Spanish media have revealed conversations between train drivers and a control centre just minutes before a deadly crash on Wednesday morning, that has killed 69 people.Officials are investigating the cause of the disaster, which occurred when a train from Madrid to Seville barrelled into a stationary train near Urda.Three audio recordings between Madrid's control centre and two train drivers appear to show that one high-speed train was given clearance to move even though another train had stalled on the track, about 25km (15 miles) ahead.Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez has said that authorities will "get to the bottom of every last detail of this tragedy".Dozens of people were injured, with survivors recounting harrowing scenes people crying and bleeding, passengers trapped in their seats, missing limbs and smoke billowing throughout the carriages, one of which caught fire.On Thursday, Spain's King Felipe VI and Queen Letizia visited some of the injured passengers in a hospital in Toledo.He later expressed condolences to the victims' relatives, pledging that the investigation would determine why the crash happened, and what measures would be taken for this not to happen again.The crash is one of the worst rail disasters in Europe's modern history, and Spain's worst crash since 2013. On Thursday, the country began three days of national mourning.The moving train, run by state-owned operator Renfe, had 397 passengers on board. The stationary train was run by private operator Iryo, and carrying 147 passengers. A reported issue with the automatic signalling system - a computer failure - had forced all trains to halt on the affected stretch.But later the Renfe train was ordered to proceed in "error", according to Spain's transport minister.The audio recordings were published by several Spanish news outlets including El Pais and RTVE.In one, a control centre operator is speaking to the driver of the Renfe train, which was having some technical difficulties. After some exchanges, the control operator tells the driver: "Continue your journey and then proceed under [Lateral Signalling Block], at normal speed with normal operation."The driver replies: "At normal speed?" To which the controller answers: "Yes."The Lateral Signalling Block is a back-up or alternative train system used when the automatic signalling or data transmission system fails.The driver of the stationary Iryo train says in another audio recording that communication with the train-control system has been lost, and it is not moving.The train "is stationary in front of the entry signal at Urda", the driver tells the control centre operator. After a series of exchanges, the driver is then told to "resume the journey" normally.The Iryo driver then contacts the control centre again, according to a later recording, saying they cannot start the train. "The train won't allow me to control the [security] system. That's why I am still stopped in front of the entry signal," they say.The latter recording suggests that the controller had been notified that the Iryo train remained stationary as the Renfe train approached.Iryo said its carriages were "struck from behind" by the other train.Spain's transport minister Óscar Puente said on Wednesday that the decision to instruct the trains to move again, without any speed restrictions, was "inexplicable".Figure caption, Watch: 'Chaotic scenes' at site of Spain's deadly train crashThe leaking of the audio recordings has been criticised by some Spanish politicians, with Alberto Ibáñez, a member of Congress for the left-wing Sumar platform, writing on X that they were "despicable".Irene Montero - the prime ministerial candidate for the left-wing Podemos party - said responsibility for the crash should not be placed on one worker, adding that train drivers and experts have been warning against the liberalisation of the railway sector for years.From the crash site, Sánchez said: "We are working day and night not only to support the victims' families, but also to establish every last detail of this tragedy and strengthen safety measures to ensure it never happens again."Most Spanish politicians have cancelled all public engagements and suspended their campaigning ahead of a snap election on 29 November.The exception is the far-right party Vox. Its leader, Santiago Abascal, said his party would not take part in what he described as attempts to "use mourning to silence criticism" of the country's rail infrastructure.Image source, Europa Press via Getty ImagesImage caption, Protesters gathered outside the transport ministry offices in Madrid on Wednesday nightOvernight, around 1,500 people gathered outside the Spanish transport ministry building in the capital, according to broadcaster TVE, which reported that demonstrators were largely calling for the resignations of Sánchez and Puente.Police used tear gas to disperse crowds after protesters hurled bottles and flares. No injuries or arrests were reported.Rail drivers went ahead with a planned strike on Thursday, with the Spanish Union of Railway Drivers (Semaf) saying the strike action was being held "in defence of railway safety". The leader of Spain's main opposition People's Party Alberto Núñez Feijóo said: "Spain has the right to know what is happening with its infrastructure."At the crash site, emergency crews worked through the night under powerful floodlights to cut open metal carriages in the search for victims, with many of those killed in the crash still to be identified.Hundreds of personnel have been deployed to the disaster site to assist with recovery efforts, Spain's interior ministry said, with drones and helicopters being used to find victims and remove rubble.A spokesperson for the Spanish Civil Guard told the BBC they had deployed more than 900 people from different specialist departments, and the priority now was identifying the deceased.They said they did not know how long this would take, but urged those with missing family members to go to one of the local centres which have been set up to offer DNA samples.

sources.headline: Spain begins mourning period as search continues for train crash victims
sources.text: Spain began three days of mourning on Thursday for at least 69 people who died in a high-speed rail collision, as hospitals continued to treat dozens of injured passengers and train drivers went on strike to urge more investment in railway safety.The trains – one from Spain’s state-owned Renfe and the other from the private rail company Iryo – were travelling from Madrid towards the southern region of Andalucía on Wednesday when they collided just before 9am. After the Iryo train came to a halt, the other slammed into its rear, knocking several carriages off the track near Urda in the central region of Castilla-La Mancha.Spain’s foreign ministry said 42 foreign citizens from seven countries were involved in the crash, adding that one had been killed and at least seven injured.Survivors shell-shocked after deadly Spain train crash - The LatestThe crash came 10 months after 46 people were killed and dozens more injured when two trains – one from Renfe and one from Iryo – collided on the same line near the town of Adamuz in Andalucía.The disaster has raised fresh questions about safety on Spain’s large, modern high-speed rail network. The transport minister, Óscar Puente, said rear-end collisions such as Wednesday’s were “highly unlikely”, and suggested the accident could have been caused by human error under “inexplicable” circumstances.Iryo employees in Madrid embrace after observing a minute’s silence for the victims of the train crash. Photograph: Bernat Armangué/APEmergency services combed the wreckage through the night for more victims, using cranes to hoist pieces of mangled metal. At daybreak, police once again launched drones to survey the crash site.Emiliano García-Page, the leader of the Castilla-La Mancha regional government, said on Thursday morning that rescue teams did not think they would find any more bodies in one damaged carriage that was ‌still overturned, but added that body parts had been found that would need to be identified.“Yesterday we experienced a catastrophe that without a doubt has left all of Spain in shock,” said García-Page. He confirmed that 50 of the people who had been taken to hospitals in the region were still being treated.The crash scene on Wednesday. Photograph: Óscar del Pozo/AFP/Getty ImagesThe prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, speaking during a visit to the emergency command centre in the city of Toledo, said the authorities were doing all they could to establish the cause of the crash and prevent another rail tragedy.“I’d like to let all Spaniards know that every institution that is part of the state – from the smallest municipality to the government of Spain – is working day and night, not only to provide a response to the families of the victims, but also, of course, to uncover every last detail of this tragedy and to strengthen safety measures so that something like this never happens again.”King Felipe, who visited a hospital in Toledo where some of the injured were being treated, said Spain had “once again suffered an extremely harsh blow” and called for lessons to be learned.“There is obviously an ongoing investigation, which should establish how and why this tragedy happened,” he said on Thursday. “Measures will need to be looked at and adopted so that this doesn’t happen again.”World Central Kitchen delivers meals to emergency services and security forces at the scene of the train collision. Photograph: Angeles Visdomine/EPAMeanwhile, Spanish train drivers went ahead with a previously planned strike to press for more investment in railway safety. The crash was Europe’s deadliest train accident since a derailment in Santiago de Compostela in north-west Spain that killed 80 people in 2013.“We will continue demanding the necessary measures to make this sector safe again ... It must have all the safety systems required to maintain the quality standards we have always had,” said Diego Martín of the train drivers’ union Semaf. “We cannot tolerate, under any circumstances, this type of incident happening again.”The Guardia Civil police force has set up four offices in the cities of Madrid, Toledo, Córdoba and Seville to enable relatives to provide DNA samples and help identify victims. Blood donation points have also been set up in Castilla-La Mancha and Madrid. The force said 64 people had been reported missing by relatives by Thursday morning.A school in Urda, which lies about 130km (80 miles) south of Madrid, has been turned into an information centre where relatives can inquire about loved ones. Teams of Red Cross workers offered support to groups of people who had arrived, some of them in tears.Carmen García, a Red Cross psychologist, said “long and hard hours” lay ahead and that “every person will manage it in their own way”. She added: “We have people who are in shock, who haven’t taken on board what has happened, angry people, sad, worried people. The grieving will be complicated.”Spain in mourning after fatal rail crash, says Spanish prime minister - videoJosé Miguel Fernández, a parish priest in Urda, joined the emergency services in offering support to the victims’ families.“It is important for relatives to find their loved ones, even if they have died, because the grieving process is quicker when you have been able to say goodbye at that final moment,” he told Onda Cero radio.Survivors have spoken of being thrown from their seats by the impact of the crash, and of trying to help the injured in the immediate aftermath.Among the first victims to be named was José Manuel Chacón, a 31-year-old Guardia Civil officer. The national law enforcement agency expressed its “deepest condolences” to his family, friends and colleagues.Also among those killed was Fátima Báñez, a former labour minister for the conservative People’s party (PP), who had gone on to chair the social and corporate responsibility arm of Spain’s ⁠employers’ association.The PP leader, Alberto Núñez Feijóo, called for an immediate investigation into what had happened, as well as a “complete and independent review” of Spain’s entire rail network. “Spain has the right to know what is going on with its infrastructure,” he told reporters.With Agence France-Presse and Reuters

'An absurdity' to blame human error: Spain's deadly train crash 'should never' have happened

Issued on: 29/10/2026 - 18:15

Share

Following Spain's deadly high-speed train crash, Delano D'Souza is joined by Francisco Badea, Director of FEM Expert Engineering, Railway Structural & PRM Certification Expert. Batea challenges explanations that reduce railway disasters to isolated human mistakes. “It is basically an absurdity to say that it depended on one person and one human mistake,” he argues, emphasizing that modern railway networks operate through multiple layers of protection, including automated safeguards, train-detection technologies, operational protocols and institutional oversight. “The system has been designed in a way that this type of accident should never happen.”

sources.headline: Spain: minute of silence for train crash victims as king visits hospital
sources.text:
Opposition People's Party leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo visited the scene, while King Felipe VI travelled to a hospital in Toledo treating survivors of the disaster. The monarch was greeted by hospital staff and other people waiting outside before entering the building.
Meanwhile, rescue teams continued searching the wreckage with sniffer dogs, as cranes lifted damaged carriages and emergency workers combed through debris scattered down a gravel embankment. One more body was recovered overnight, bringing the death toll to 69, according to Castilla-La Mancha regional president Emiliano García-Page, who said 50 people remained in hospital.
The collision occurred on Wednesday morning when a high-speed train operated by state-owned Renfe struck the rear of a stationary Iryo service in central Spain. At least three carriages were thrown down an embankment by the impact.
The government declared three days of national mourning from Thursday, as the country's second deadly high-speed rail disaster this year raised fresh questions about railway safety.
In January, 46 people were killed in another collision involving Renfe and Iryo trains on the same line. The latest crash, just four weeks before a national election, has also disrupted rail travel, with the high-speed route between Madrid and Seville closed and thousands of passengers seeking alternative transport.

sources.headline: Spain reckons with 2nd deadly train crash of the year ahead of national election
sources.text:
Emergency services work at the scene of a collision between two trains in Urda, Spain, on Wednesday, Oct. 28, 2026.
Manu Fernandez/AP
hide caption
Manu Fernandez/AP
URDA, Spain — Spain's second high-speed rail disaster this year, a crash in which one train struck another from behind, killing 68 people, has raised fresh concerns about the safety of the country's rail network. Spain's network of high-speed rail has been considered one of the nation's crowning achievements. It ranks second to China in track mileage in the world. Until this year, it had not endured a deadly crash since coming into service over three decades ago. The collision Wednesday that turned a sleepy stretch of rail lined by olive groves into a scene of carnage came just four weeks before the country votes in a national election.
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez visited the crash site in the central province of Toledo after regional authorities confirmed that more than 60 people had died and dozens more were being treated at hospitals. Only in January, 46 people had died when one train jumped the track and slammed into the side of another going the opposite way in southern Spain.
The graphic above shows the placement of derailed train cars from both trains after the crash and the events leading to the crash.
Phil Holm/AP
hide caption
Phil Holm/AP
Sánchez pledged an investigation into the latest collision and improvements to prevent another tragedy like the two that have shaken trust in a rail system that carried 45 million travelers last year, including millions of tourists. "It is clear that we need to reinforce the safety of our train service to rebuild the trust in our high-speed rail," Sánchez said. "It is not acceptable for a country like Spain to endure two high-speed train accidents in the same year." Sánchez's government declared three days of mourning starting Thursday. Both deadly crashes this year involved a train operated by the state-owned RENFE company and one from the privately owned IRYO. Spain only liberalized its high-speed rail service in 2021, with the Italian IRYO starting service the following year. Political implications for Sánchez ahead of election Sánchez has weathered many crises since taking power in 2018, staying in power and winning reelection after the COVID-19 pandemic and the global rise in inflation.
But polls show he faces another uphill battle when voters cast ballots in Spain's first national election since 2023. The new rail disaster can't help the prospects of his Socialist party. Sánchez and other progressive parties had hoped to leverage a wave of discontent over housing costs and high rents when he called for early elections earlier this month. About an hour before news of Wednesday's crash spread, Sánchez had posted on X a message that "There are lots of reasons to be optimistic about this country." Now it appears he will have to handle concerns over the state of Spain's rail service along with attacks from right-wing parties over his liberal migration policies and accusations of corruption against his party and his wife, which both he and his wife deny. His transport minister, Óscar Puente, had to handle media questions over whether he would resign following a second major train wreck under his watch. His response was that he was fully focused on dealing with the collision, not his future. Sánchez's main rival, Popular Party leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo, demanded a full investigation of the crash. The conservative leader said that in respect for the victims his party canceled its campaign events for the day. "This is the moment to respect the dead, the injured and their families," Núñez Feijóo said. "That does not mean we will ignore the fact that Spaniards are asking tough questions that demand answers." The far-right Vox leader, Santiago Abascal, who is likely hoping to enter a coalition government with the conservatives, did not show the same restraint. "More dead. Another tragedy. More rage over being left to fend for ourselves, the despair and the betrayal that Spaniards are enduring," Abascal said just hours after the crash. "I promise to work tirelessly until this government, which is a criminal organization, is sitting in a courtroom to answer for its crimes," he said.
Emergency services work at the scene of a collision between two trains in Urda, Spain, on Wednesday, Oct. 28, 2026.
Manu Fernandez/AP
hide caption
Manu Fernandez/AP
Human error was behind the crash Puente said that the crash was caused by what he called the "inexplicable" order from a central command center for Spain's trains after a security system had failed. He said the train engineers were not to blame.
Puente said that at 8:30 a.m. the security system on a stretch of 63 kilometers (39 miles) stopped working due to a computer malfunction, causing all trains on that stretch to stop. At that point the IRYO train was stopped near the town of Urda, while the RENFE train was 25 kilometers (15.5 miles) behind it. But a few minutes later the central command told the RENFE train to start running again without any speed restrictions, and it ended up colliding with the stationary IRYO train at 8:53 a.m. Puente said that the train should never have been told to start moving again since there was still a "stop signal" active on that line. And if it had, at least it should have been told to go at reduced speed. Workers started to use cranes to move parts of the damaged trains late on Wednesday after a hectic day involving hundreds of emergency workers, firefighters, police and soldiers all pitching in to rescue survivors and recover bodies.

sources.headline: Spain train crash survivor recalls scenes of devastation as accident unfolded
sources.text: MADRID – When his train drew to a halt, Sebastian Herrero thought the stoppage was due to a fallen overhead line, a problem that has increasingly beset Spain’s high-speed railway network in recent years.But concerns about arriving late at his destination were suddenly interrupted when he found himself flying through the air and landing face-first on the seat opposite as another train slammed into the back of his.Herrero, 46, was on his way on Oct 28 to Seville from Madrid on an early-morning train operated by Iryo when a train operated by state-owned Renfe ploughed into it, sending its final three carriages careering down a raised embankment in a crash that killed 69 people.Herrero and others in his carriage escaped by scrambling down the embankment and crossing a fence into a field. Looking back, he realised the extent of the accident for the first time.“The scene was devastating. You saw carriages completely burnt out, as if they’d exploded.“What you see coming out were people in a very bad way, and others who start pulling out the bodies of the deceased and placing them right there next to where we were,” Herrero said in an interview in Seville.Herrero, who said he feels “born again” after surviving the disaster, was fortunate that his carriage was near the front of the train, but the impact still left many passengers with broken arms or noses.Dilemma after January crashThe crash followed another accident that killed dozens in January and involved the same rail companies on the same line near the town of Adamuz.It has revived a debate about safety and maintenance on Spain’s high-speed rail network, Europe’s longest and – until recently – a source of pride for Spaniards.Herrero remembers people asking him after the Adamuz accident whether he felt safe taking the train.“I remember when the Adamuz thing happened because I spent a month and a half thinking about lots of things, as I had to drive there and the roads aren’t exactly in the best condition either,” he said.“Petrol isn’t at its cheapest right now, far from it, and flying isn’t an option. So for many of us who have that connection between Seville and Madrid and whose lives depend on it, you can’t see any other solution.”For many of the people of different nationalities and backgrounds involved in the Oct 28 accident, the prevailing feeling was one of indignation.“It is high time for whoever is responsible to take responsibility,” Herrero said.“I don’t know whether it is up to the courts to say so, or whether it is up to politicians, or whether it is for the Spanish people to decide, but what is clear is that it is unacceptable for this to happen and it is inconceivable that it could ever happen again,” he added. REUTERS

sources.headline: Crash survivors recount chaotic scenes in Europe's worst train disaster since 2013
sources.text: Residents of a rural village in central Spain have raced to provide help after Europe's deadliest rail disaster in more than a decade.At least 68 people were killed and dozens more were injured when two high-speed trains carrying hundreds of passengers between Madrid and Seville collided in the Toledo province on Wednesday, local time. A train operated by the state-owned RENFE company struck the rear of another train operated by private company IRYO that was stationery.The collision derailed two carriages on the tail of the Iryo train and the front of the RENFE train.The crash occurred on a flat stretch surrounded by olive fields between the villages of Urda and Los Yébenes, shredding carriages into bits of metal and other material.Debris was scattered down a gravel slope.Dozens of passengers were also injured in the crash and taken to an Urda sport centre converted into a triage treatment hub. (AP: Andrea Comas)In Urda, 78-year-old pharmacist Antonioa Garcia told Reuters he was among the first on the scene, jumping into his car to help after his daughter told him about the crash.He said that as he neared the crash site, the scale of the accident became clear when he saw one carriage wedged inside another and scores of bodies."Just imagine what was inside," he said.Relatives of people who were aboard the train at the time of the crash travelled to the crash site in search of their family members. (AP: Andrea Comas)The pharmacist said he brought first-aid materials, painkillers and tranquillisers from his pharmacy, as well as blankets, to help treat the injured.He also described how one passenger who had lost an arm in the crash was calmly asking for an ambulance, while another was saying his final goodbyes to his family.The front carriage of one of the trains was severed after derailing following the collision. (ABC News: Ryan Boyle)"His last words were, 'God is good'. For those of us who are believers, these are very beautiful words," Mr Garcia said.Other locals brought bottles of water to give to passengers who were evacuated from the two trains.Construction worker David Gómez was also working nearby when he heard the crash and ran to help, he told the newspaper El País."People were trying to get out through the windows … We cut through some fences to access the area and treated people with the first-aid kits we had brought until emergency services arrived," he said."As I was trying to pull a young woman out, there was a piece of a leg."The RENFE train rounded a bend in the railway leading up to the location of the stationary Iryo carriage. (ABC News: Ryan Boyle)Another survivor told reporters at the scene that he was standing close to a carriage door at the time of the crash."Passengers were breaking the glass to get out. Some people couldn't move because they were trapped among the seats," he said.A visibly shaken Manuel Ortiz, who lives in Urda, told AFP he had been transporting survivors all morning in his car.The two trains were derailed on either side of an embankment after the collision. (AP: Manu Fernandez)The 49-year-old described a "horrific, horrible" scene that "smelled of an accident, of metal".Ambulances and medical helicopters made trips to and from the site, while buses took survivors who were unharmed. A military emergency brigade was deployed to help.The crash is the second deadly rail incident in Spain since January, and the worst in Europe in more than a decade. (AFP: Oscar Del Pozo)Australian Education Minister Jason Clare said the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade (DFAT) was not aware of any Australians who had been affected by the crash."As you'd expect, we've got consular officials in Spain who stand ready to help any Australians or any Australian families if they are affected," he told the ABC."I think the whole country is in shock at the moment, seeing these images on our screens. [They're] just horrific."In a statement, DFAT offered its condolences to victims' families and other people affected by the collision.Passengers' moments of chaosSamy Paul, a British tourist, was aboard the RENFE train at the time of the crash and described the shock of the impact to The Associated Press after being rescued."Suddenly, everything started falling apart. Bang! We fell down," he said."We realised carriage two, carriage one, all gone, all smashed. There was blood all over."Members of the Spanish Red Cross helped to comfort family members of passengers who were waiting for news from the crash site. (Reuters: Susana Vera)Passenger Ignacio Relaño was also travelling on the RENFE train. He told state broadcaster TVE the train stopped momentarily on the line, then started again and crashed into the IRYO train."We all felt the train abruptly slowing down and then the impact," he said."The car leaned to one side like it was about to tip over. I hit my nose, everything went flying, luggage, cell phones. Everything shook."Pablo Mejia, 42, told AFP he had miraculously survived with injuries to his head after changing his seat.With blood staining his grey jumper, he recounted "a very strong hit"."It lasted a long time until it stopped, lots of people on the floor, on top of each other, seats ripped out, suitcases, a lot of chaos," he said.'Devastating' search for family membersA few hours after the crash, Urda was filled with police, firefighters and emergency workers from across the region, and the local sports hall was converted into a centre for survivors.The local primary school was reserved for relatives of the victims, where a volunteer psychologist from Madrid named Carmen said she had been helping out since the morning."There were many mothers who found out their children had been killed," she said."That was the worst of today. Telling a mother that her child has died in a train crash is devastating."Some relatives made the two-hour trip from Madrid, the Spanish capital, to search for family members.A woman who gave her name as Ana said she travelled to Urda after environmental police called to say they had found her dog, Trece, who was on board a train with her husband, Pepe.Ana fought back tears as she described searching for her husband at the crash site, Urda's sports hall and the primary school, adding that his name was not on any list.Expat journalist Chris Havler-Barrett told the ABC he had spent most of the day at the triage centre in Urda, which he described as "quite harrowing"."[We] could hear the grief and cries of family who were receiving news on what must have been the worst day of their life," he said."It's an apocalyptic scene this country was not prepared for."Mr Havler-Barrett said Spain's rail system was very busy at the time of the crash as people sought to travel before planned industrial action strikes on Thursday.He also said the disaster occurred ahead of the busiest travel weekend of the year in Spain, as residents return home for All Saints Day.Rescue workers continue to scour the wreckage of the two trains in search of survivors and bodies of victims.The collision is the deadliest in Europe since a 2013 crash in Spain's Santiago de Compostela left 80 people dead.Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez has declared three days of national mourning and called for increased safety measures to restore confidence in the country's high-speed rail system.ABC/wires
